mcqs.question: After a security review, every JSON route returns `Cache-Control: no-store` next to its `ETag`. A teammate argues this is harmless because the `ETag` still lets clients revalidate. A week later egress on the endpoint is unchanged and the `304` rate is zero: every poll is a full `200`. What explains it?
options: `no-store` forbids storing the response in any cache, so there is no copy left to revalidate; `no-cache` stores it and forces validation before every reuse.
`no-store` only binds shared caches, so the CDN stops storing while browsers keep their copy; the missing `304`s come from the CDN, not the client.
`no-store` needs `must-revalidate` next to it; without that flag clients skip `If-None-Match` and refetch the whole representation.
`If-None-Match` is only honoured for cache entries keyed by `Vary`, so that header has to be added before any `304` can be produced.
mcqs.explanation: A `304` answers a conditional request, and a conditional request exists only because a cache stored the earlier response together with its validator. `no-store` says a cache MUST NOT store any part of the response, and RFC 9111 makes that apply to private and shared caches alike (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html#section-5.2.2.5), so the browser has nothing to hold an `ETag` against and every poll goes out unconditional; the validator is present on the wire and never used. `no-cache` is the directive that does what the team wanted: the response may be stored but MUST be validated before each reuse (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html#section-5.2.2.4), and the server side of that exchange is `If-None-Match` with a `304` (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-13.1.2). The strongest distractor is the private-versus-shared reading, because the distinction is real - `private` and `s-maxage` genuinely separate the two cache classes - and it is exactly the leap that makes `no-store` look narrow, yet it is the one storage directive that binds both. `must-revalidate` governs what a cache does with an already-stored stale response and cannot create a stored copy, and `Vary` selects among stored variants instead of gating the conditional request.

mcqs.question: A legacy internal dashboard is served over HTTP/1.1 through a proxy that never negotiates h2. It opens one `EventSource` per panel - now eight - and uses `fetch` for actions. After the last two panels shipped, actions hang for tens of seconds and complete only when a panel is closed. Server CPU, event-loop lag and database metrics are all idle. What explains the hang?
options: Each `EventSource` is an HTTP response that never ends, and HTTP/1.1 allows about six connections per origin, so eight streams exhaust the pool and `fetch` waits; share one stream routed by event name, or use HTTP/2.
Each `EventSource` performs a WebSocket upgrade, and the proxy admits only one upgraded connection per client, so the extra panels queue behind a handshake that never completes and its retries.
The eight open responses pin the Node event loop, so the process cannot read the action requests off the socket until one stream closes and its callbacks are released.
The streams reconnect every few seconds; those retries occupy the connection slots, so the actions wait behind the reconnect attempts instead of a free socket.
mcqs.explanation: An `EventSource` is not a special transport: it is an ordinary `GET` whose `text/event-stream` response never finishes, so it occupies a connection for as long as it is open. Outside HTTP/2 the browser caps simultaneous connections per origin at a very low number - six, as MDN's server-sent events guide states while noting that HTTP/2 removes the limit because streams are negotiated (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Server-sent_events/Using_server-sent_events) - so the seventh and eighth streams queue, and the `fetch` behind them waits in the browser's per-origin pool without a request ever reaching the server. That is why every server metric is idle: the stall is client-side scheduling, not work. The standard fix is one stream per tab with the server naming events so a single listener can route them, or serving the dashboard over HTTP/2 where the streams multiplex; the bank's own WS-versus-SSE table carries the same caveat. The strongest distractor is the event-loop one, because 'Node is single-threaded' and 'eight long responses must be expensive' both sound like engineering common sense, but an open stream with no data costs a socket, not CPU, and a blocked event loop would show lag, elevated loop delay and stalled requests on every route including plain page loads. `EventSource` is not an upgrade mechanism, so the handshake option describes WebSocket, and `retry:` only governs the delay after a drop - a healthy stream holds its slot legitimately, which is the same root cause stated correctly.

mcqs.question: For a credentialed cross-origin fetch, which response is valid?
options: Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with no other header
An explicit allowed origin plus Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true
No CORS headers because cookies imply authorization
Only Access-Control-Allow-Methods on the actual response
mcqs.explanation: Credentialed requests require an explicit allowed origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true for the response to be exposed. The best distractor is the wildcard: browsers reject the wildcard for credentialed responses.

mcqs.question: A public, non-personalized `/config` is cached for five minutes at a CDN. The origin reflects the caller's `Origin` when it is one of 400 partner origins and sends `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. Symptom one: some partners get a response their browser blocks. Symptom two: after someone adds `Vary: Origin`, the CDN hit rate collapses. Which reading is right?
options: Missing `Vary: Origin` caused the misdelivery, and 400 origins is why it is not the fix: keep the body origin-neutral and let the edge add the allowlisted header, so variants stay bounded.
`Vary: Origin` partitions the wrong field - CORS answers vary with `Accept-Encoding` because compression rewrites headers - so the hit rate fell for an unrelated reason.
Key the CDN on the `Origin` request header instead of sending `Vary`, because `Vary` is only honoured by browser caches and a shared cache ignores it.
Nothing here is wrong: with 400 variants the drop is cache warming, so keep `Vary: Origin` and lengthen the TTL until every variant has been stored once.
mcqs.explanation: A shared cache keys on the URL unless `Vary` tells it otherwise, so a reflected `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` was stored under `GET /config` and handed to the next origin to ask, which is exactly the blocked response the partners saw; and what makes that response origin-specific is the header, not the body, so `Vary: Origin` really does make the reflection safe (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Caching). The catch is cardinality: `Vary` multiplies stored copies by distinct `Origin`, which is fine for a handful of first-party origins and ruinous for 400, because each copy is requested rarely and expires before it is reused again - hence the collapsed hit rate. The durable answer is to stop reflecting: serve one origin-neutral representation and add the allowlisted header at the edge from its own configuration, or issue a fixed per-origin response, so the variant space stays bounded while the origin response stays cacheable. The strongest distractor is the 'key the CDN on `Origin` instead of `Vary`' option, because it sounds like the same partition done natively and faster; it is the same partition with identical cardinality, and its premise - that shared caches ignore `Vary` - is false. `Accept-Encoding` genuinely belongs in `Vary` on compressed responses, which is what makes that option feel familiar, but it is a different axis and could not have produced a mismatched allow origin.

mcqs.question: Room events are published by whichever of three Node instances handled the HTTP write, and each instance holds the WebSocket connections that happened to land on it behind a round-robin load balancer. Local single-instance runs are fine; in production about two thirds of room members never receive an event, while CPU, memory and event-loop lag stay flat. Which change fixes the delivery?
options: Sockets live in one process, so an event published on another process reaches nobody: publish to a shared bus that every instance subscribes to, and let each instance write to the sockets it owns.
Enable sticky sessions so every member stays on one instance for the life of the socket; the publishing instance can then reach that member's connection directly.
Raise the per-connection send buffer and the instance's open-file limit; the events are being dropped by backpressure in the publisher's queue before they reach a socket.
Move every WebSocket upgrade onto a single, larger instance so fan-out is local, and let the other two instances keep serving plain HTTP writes.
mcqs.explanation: A WebSocket connection belongs to the process that accepted it, and there is no cross-process handle to it; with round-robin, a publish handled by instance A reaches only the third of the room that is connected to A, which is precisely the one-third success rate reported. The fix is to invert the direction: producers publish to a bus every instance subscribes to (Redis pub/sub, NATS, Kafka) and each instance performs the local fan-out over its own sockets, with a shared sequence number or snapshot path so a client that reconnects elsewhere can catch up. The strongest distractor is sticky sessions, because affinity is a real WebSocket technique and it does sound like it makes 'the publishing instance reach the member' - but the publisher is chosen by the HTTP write, not by the member, so affinity only makes a client's home predictable; it still needs a transport from A's process to B's socket, and it breaks every time a deploy or autoscale event moves a client anyway, which is why the bank frames affinity as an optimization rather than the answer. Buffer and file-descriptor limits are a different failure: they show memory growth, `send()` queue depth or `EMFILE` errors, and they would degrade gradually rather than silencing exactly the members on other instances - and note the browser side has no blocking backpressure at all, it just accumulates and reports `bufferedAmount` (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSocket/bufferedAmount), so per-connection queues must be bounded server-side whatever the topology. Concentrating every socket on one instance trades three processes for one and reintroduces the deploy-time reconnect storm the cluster existed to avoid.

mcqs.question: An app runs over HTTP/2 on one origin. Under 0.5% packet loss, users report that a burst of small API calls sits idle behind a single large upload, even though the calls are separate streams. A teammate says multiplexing already solved this and blames the server's concurrency. What actually explains the stalls, and what does HTTP/3 change?
options: Multiplexing only applies inside one response, so the fix on either protocol is six parallel connections per origin, as in HTTP/1.1.
The stalls are a server concurrency problem: HTTP/2 applies flow control per stream and TCP retransmission is invisible to HTTP, so the ceiling is the connection's max concurrent streams.

HTTP/2 removes application-level head-of-line blocking but still delivers one ordered TCP byte stream, so a lost segment stalls every multiplexed stream until it is retransmitted; HTTP/3 runs each stream over QUIC, where a gap on one stream does not block the others.
HTTP/3 must be requested explicitly by the application by switching to an `h3://` URL scheme, so until the app does that the client correctly keeps HTTP/2 transport behavior.
mcqs.explanation: HTTP/2 fixed the HTTP/1.1 queue - requests no longer wait for earlier responses to finish - but every stream still shares one TCP connection, and TCP delivers bytes in order, so a lost segment holds back all streams until retransmission (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html). HTTP/3 carries HTTP over QUIC, where each stream is delivered and flow-controlled independently, and TLS 1.3 is part of the handshake (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9114.html, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9000.html). The strongest distractor is the flow-control answer: HTTP/2 does have per-stream flow-control windows (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9113.html#section-5.2), so the vocabulary is real, but a window governs how much data one stream may have in flight - it cannot deliver bytes past a missing segment, so raising stream limits or worker counts changes nothing about the stall. The six-connections option describes HTTP/1.1 workarounds that HTTP/2 exists to replace, and there is no `h3://` scheme: HTTP/3 is negotiated for an `https://` origin, and blocked UDP makes a client fall back to TCP-based HTTP rather than requiring an app change.

mcqs.question: A dashboard receives SSE updates and applies them from a queue flushed on a 250 ms timer, so an event can be parsed but not yet applied. The connection drops mid-batch, `EventSource` reconnects, and the server resumes from the value in `Last-Event-ID`. What gap risk does that header carry here?
options: None: `Last-Event-ID` names the last event the listener finished handling, so the reconnect replays exactly the unfinished batch.

`Last-Event-ID` reports the last id the stream delivered - set when the browser dispatches the event, before your listener returns - so an event already received but not yet applied can be skipped by the resumed stream; keep your own applied cursor and replay or resync from it.
`Last-Event-ID` is sent as a query parameter on reconnect, so a server that reads the request headers sees nothing and replays the whole history every time.
`EventSource` clears the remembered id after any successful reconnect, so resumption only works for the first drop and later reconnects start from scratch.
mcqs.explanation: The spec sets the event source's last event ID string while dispatching an event, from the stream's `id` field, and the value persists until the server sets a new one; on reconnect that string becomes the `Last-Event-ID` request header, and only then does the server choose what to replay (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html). Delivery bookkeeping is therefore not application acknowledgement: anything sitting in your queue when the socket dies is beyond the cursor the server is told about, and a server that resumes strictly after that cursor will never resend it. Persisting your own applied position - and having a defined recovery path such as a snapshot fetch when that position is older than the replay window - is what makes the queue safe (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/EventSource). The strongest distractor is the acknowledgement reading: it is the intuitive mental model ("last id means last one I dealt with") and it is exactly the assumption that turns a reconnect into silent data loss when batching, debouncing, or any async apply sits in front of the stream. The query-parameter option has the location wrong - it is a request header - and the clearing option is wrong too: an explicit empty `id` field resets the cursor, but a successful reconnect does not.

mcqs.question: `POST /reports` runs a four-minute warehouse query and returns `200` with the generated PDF when it finishes. In production the proxy answers `504` at 60 seconds, clients retry the same POST and create duplicate reports, and a user who reloads the page cannot retrieve the report that was already built. Which change addresses all three symptoms?
options: Raise the proxy and load-balancer timeouts past four minutes and turn off automatic retries on the route, so the original request can carry the result.
Respond `200` with an empty body immediately and write the PDF to a shared folder; the client then polls that folder by filename until the file appears.
Stream the response as `text/plain` progress lines and finish with the PDF, so the connection proves liveness and no separate status resource is needed.

Respond `202 Accepted` with an operation id and a monitor URL, make the start request idempotent for retries, and treat a durable status resource - states, progress, eventual error - as the source of truth, observed by polling with backoff or a push channel.
mcqs.explanation: `202 Accepted` means accepted for processing, not completed or guaranteed to succeed, so the response owes the client an operation identifier and a URL to check, and the status resource must expose the eventual outcome and errors (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html#section-15.3.3). That single design answers all three symptoms: the request returns long before any proxy deadline, an idempotent start keyed by the caller prevents the retry duplicate, and the durable operation outlives the reload so the result is retrievable later. The strongest distractor is raising the timeout: it can be made to work for one happy path, but it keeps the work tied to a socket - a deploy, a client disconnect, or a terminal-less retry still loses the result, and nothing makes the retried POST safe. The empty-200 option replaces the contract with an out-of-band convention and gives no authorization or failure channel, and streaming progress is a presentation choice rather than a recovery path: the status resource stays necessary for a client that was not connected when the job finished.

scenarios.prompt: A CDN sits in front of an API whose `/profile` route returns per-user JSON. This function builds its CORS and cache headers. Three reports came in after the CDN warmed: (1) a user opened their profile and saw another account's email and phone; (2) an origin that is not on `ALLOWED` received a response whose `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` named `https://app.example`; (3) purging the CDN cleared both for about an hour. Rewrite the header policy and draw the cache boundary so the first two cannot return, and say what `Vary: Origin` would and would not fix here.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
There are two independent defects and the prompt's third symptom is the proof that they are cache defects rather than a rendering bug: purging the edge clears them, so what users saw was a stored copy.

**Defect 1 - a shared cache is allowed to store per-user data.** `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60` on `/profile` declares the representation reusable by any cache, and a shared cache keys on the URL, not on the session cookie or `req.user`. The first user's JSON is stored under `GET /profile` and served to everyone inside the minute, and the CDN may serve it long after that if the entry is revalidated or refreshed. That is symptom 1.

**Defect 2 - the header names an origin the request never earned.** `ALLOWED.has(origin) ? origin : 'https://app.example'` is worse than a missing header: for an origin that is not allowlisted the server asserts that `https://app.example` is the permitted origin. The browser at that other origin then compares its own origin with `https://app.example`, fails, and blocks a body the server had already authorized in a header. Only the browser's check stood between that response and a reader, and CORS was never an authorization boundary for state changes in the first place. That is symptom 2, and it is visible with `curl -H 'Origin: https://evil.example'`.

**Fix the policy, then the boundary.**

1. Per-user responses do not go in the shared cache: `Cache-Control: private, no-store` (or `private, max-age=0, must-revalidate` if the browser is allowed to keep the copy), plus a CDN rule that bypasses `/profile`. `private` alone excludes shared caches; `no-store` is the stronger choice when the data is sensitive and you do not want it on disk (https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111.html#section-5.2.2.5).
2. Emit CORS headers only for allowlisted origins: if `ALLOWED.has(origin)` is false, send neither `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` nor `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`, and let the browser block. Never substitute a default origin. Keep the explicit origin - `*` is invalid with credentials - and keep the route's own per-user authorization, because a blocked response still means the request was processed.
3. `Vary: Origin` is not the repair here. It partitions cached variants of one URL by `Origin`, which is the correct fix for a cacheable response whose *headers* differ per origin (public config, preflights); it does nothing about the representation differing per *user*, and once the response is `no-store` there is no stored copy for `Vary` to key. Adding it to `/profile` would leave symptom 1 untouched while looking like a fix.

**Verify through the intermediary, not against the origin.** Two users on two origins, CDN cold then warm, checking `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`, `Cache-Control`, `Vary` and `X-Cache`/`Age` on each hop, plus a non-allowlisted origin expecting no CORS headers at all.
rubric: Separates the two failures: cross-user leakage is a shared-cache decision, while the wrong `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` is a header the server should not have emitted at all.
Takes per-user data out of the shared cache (`private`/`no-store`, plus an edge rule for the path) instead of trying to make the shared entry safe.
Omits the CORS headers for non-allowlisted origins rather than defaulting to one, keeps an explicit origin with credentials, and keeps authorization on the route.
Explains that `Vary: Origin` partitions cached variants by origin, cannot make per-user data shareable, and is moot once nothing is stored.
Validates the result through the CDN with two origins and two users, cold and warm, including a non-allowlisted origin.

scenarios.prompt: This consumer powers a dashboard. The server writes every message as an `event: update` block with `data: {"id":"...","value":...}`, sets an `id:` on each one, and sends a `retry: 5000` line; the proxy closes connections idle for 30 seconds. Three reports came in: (1) the stream opens, the server logs the subscription, and no panel ever changes; (2) after a laptop sleeps and wakes, rows appear twice; (3) a reconnect after a two-minute gap leaves the board stale until a manual reload, even though the server resumes from `Last-Event-ID` for the last 60 seconds only. Fix the consumer so the first two stop happening and the third has a defined recovery, without fighting the browser's own reconnection.
scenarios.modelAnswer:
Symptom 1 is a wire-format mismatch, not a network problem. `onmessage` is only invoked for events with no `event:` field; the server names them `update`, so the browser dispatches an `update`-typed event that nothing listens to (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Server-sent_events/Using_server-sent_events). The connection is healthy, which is why the server log looks fine. The fix is `source.addEventListener('update', handler)`, and any other `event:` name the server introduces gets its own listener or a single dispatcher that switches on `event.type`.

Symptom 2 is replay semantics. On reconnect the browser sends `Last-Event-ID` and the server resumes from its own cursor, so anything between the drop and the reconnect can be delivered twice, and nothing in the protocol promises exactly-once. Treat the stream as at-least-once: key applied updates by `event.lastEventId || update.id`, keep a bounded set of recently applied ids, and make the apply step idempotent. If two updates carry the same id, the later value wins rather than appending a second row.

Symptom 3 is the retention boundary. `Last-Event-ID` is only meaningful inside the server's 60-second replay window; a two-minute gap means the cursor cannot be honoured, and a server that quietly starts at the live tail produces a board that looks connected but is stale. The consumer needs its own recovery path: record when the connection was lost (or watch `source.readyState` and `onerror`), and on reconnect past the window - or when the server sends an explicit `event: reset` - fetch `/dashboard/snapshot`, replace the board with it, and then apply only events newer than the snapshot's cursor. Replay is the fast path; the snapshot is the correctness boundary.

What I would not change: the browser's reconnection. `EventSource` retries with backoff honouring `retry:`, and closing and recreating the source in `onerror` throws away both the cursor and that backoff. Keep the returned cleanup and call it on `pagehide` and on route change so a forgotten stream does not leak a connection. Two transport details belong on the server: a comment heartbeat (for example `: ping` every 15 seconds) so the 30-second proxy timeout never fires on an idle but healthy stream, and `Cache-Control: no-store` plus buffering disabled so no intermediary accumulates events. Finally, an expired session is not a network error - surface re-authentication instead of letting an invisible retry loop run forever.
rubric: Names the type mismatch explicitly: `onmessage` never fires for `event: update`, so the dead panels become `addEventListener('update', ...)` rather than a hunt for a network fault.
Parses defensively and validates the payload instead of casting `JSON.parse(event.data)` straight to `Update`.
Treats replay as at-least-once and dedupes by `lastEventId`/update id, applying updates idempotently.
Defines recovery past the 60-second replay window (fetch a snapshot, then apply events newer than its cursor) instead of trusting `Last-Event-ID` indefinitely.
Leaves reconnection to `EventSource`, cleans up on `pagehide`/route change, and covers the idle-timeout and buffering details on the server side.

scenarios.prompt: This SSE endpoint powers a dashboard over a private network where tunnels drop every few minutes. After a deploy, three symptoms appear: (1) reconnecting browsers replay the entire day of events, spiking CPU; (2) some clients skip updates and never notice; (3) a client that reconnects after a five-minute outage shows a stale board until a manual reload. The author insists resume is implemented because the handler honours `?since=`. Find the defects in cursor handling, replay and live subscription, and rewrite the handler so resumption is actually correct - including what to send when the cursor cannot be honoured.
rubric: Identifies that the events carry no `id`, so the browser never sends `Last-Event-ID` and the advertised `?since=` resume is unreachable rather than merely miswired.
Reads the cursor from the `Last-Event-ID` request header (case-insensitively, as client-supplied and untrusted) instead of a query parameter.
Closes the replay-to-live gap atomically, so events committed between the end of the backlog and the subscription are neither dropped nor duplicated.
Bounds replay by retention and falls back to a labelled snapshot plus a fresh cursor for unknown or expired cursors instead of silently starting at the live tail.
States at-least-once delivery with client-side reconciliation by id, and keeps the connection alive and leak-free (heartbeat, cache and buffering headers, cleanup on `close`).
